title: Three-Way Inference Buyers Guide for Platform Teams
body:
Audience:
- Platform engineering, infra/platform architects, and internal procurement teams evaluating managed inference endpoints (hyperscaler-managed endpoints vs Redwood Dedicated/Private).

Purpose / TL;DR:
- Practical three-way comparison (AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints) vs Redwood’s product modes (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private). Focused on the operational tradeoffs platform teams care about: control, performance predictability, cost transparency, rollout & versioning, security/compliance, and vendor lock-in risk.

Key buyer personas and their top signals:
- Platform Owner (SRE/Platform): uptime SLOs, consistent p99 latency, traffic shaping, observability hooks, and predictable capacity scaling.
- Security/Compliance Lead: VPC/SOC controls, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, and data residency.
- Product/ML Platform Engineer: model versioning, canary rollouts, performance regression detection, reproducible evals, and kernel/quantization options.
- Procurement/Finance: unit economics, cost predictability, committed discounts vs pay-as-you-go, and transparency into what drives cost.

Decision Axes (how platform teams decide) and what matters operationally:
1) Control & Abstraction Boundaries:
   - Hyperscalers: strong control-plane integration with other cloud services but limited low-level serving knobs (kernel selection, batching internals). Control often tied to cloud account constructs and IAM.
   - Redwood: unified API consistent across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Deeper serving runtime controls (batching, KV caching, fallback policies) and ability to pin model versions with rollout policies separated from infra.

2) Predictability & Latency Guarantees:
   - Hyperscalers: soft p99s vary by region and instance class; burst behavior depends on underlying autoscaling mechanisms. Latency SLAs often coarse.
   - Redwood Dedicated: predictable throughput backed by commit contracts; autoscaling policies tuned for inference patterns; explicit fallbacks to compatible model variants to preserve availability under pressure.

3) Cost Visibility & Unit Economics:
   - Hyperscalers: pricing opaque—instance types, underlying GPU multiplexing, and managed service margins make per-token/unit cost estimation harder.
   - Redwood: instrumentation at token-call level, route/model-level cost breakouts, and Optimize suggestions (batching, quantization) tied to measured savings.

4) Security & Compliance:
   - Hyperscalers: mature cloud security stack; however cross-account integrations and data flows can complicate compliance for regulated customers. Private connectivity often requires complex network engineering.
   - Redwood Private: designed for air-gapped or VPC-first deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging designed around inference events.

5) Model Lifecycle & Rollouts:
   - Hyperscalers: model registry features exist but rollout tooling is often generic. Canary routing and rollback may require glue code.
   - Redwood: first-class rollout constructs for inference (canary by traffic percent, A/B, automatic regressions tied to eval prompts) and built-in fallbacks for graceful degradation.

Comparative bullet summary (platform-team speak):
- If you want maximal integration with existing cloud infra and are comfortable trading off low-level serving control: hyperscalers are convenient.
- If your priority is deterministic p99/p50 behavior, transparent per-request economics, and operational levers to tune cost/latency at the model-serving layer: Redwood Dedicated/Private is the better fit.
- If you need fast time-to-prototype with low ops friction and can accept variable economics: Redwood Hosted API or hyperscaler managed endpoints both possible — choose based on contract and data controls.

Narrow win themes and sales talk tracks (short scripts):
1) For platform teams worried about unpredictable p99 spikes:
   "We treat inference as a first-class runtime: dedicated GPU pools + traffic-aware batching and fallbacks. That means your p99 becomes a predictable engineering target rather than a surprise month-end bill."

2) For security/compliance buyers evaluating private deployments:
   "The control plane can live in your VPC or on-prem; keys stay in your KMS/HSM. You get both the operational tooling of a managed platform and the boundary controls of a private deployment."

3) For finance/procurement comparing per-token costs:
   "We instrument down to route+model level and provide Optimize recommendations that map directly to expected $/request savings — enabling predictable commit sizing for Dedicated contracts."

Objection handling (common hyperscaler pushbacks):
- "But hyperscalers already run our infra": emphasize lock-in, granular observability limits, and the difficulty of matching inference economics across multiple teams. Offer a migration/side-by-side test plan.
- "We can build this in-house": counter with total cost of ownership: engineering effort to maintain inference runtime, benchmarked cost at scale, and the risk of regressions without integrated eval tooling.
- "We need multi-region failover baked into cloud infra": show Redwood’s smart routing and region-aware fallbacks plus examples of cross-region rollout strategies used by customers.

Recommended evaluation checklist (deliverable for POC):
- Benchmarks: run identical prompts through hyperscaler managed endpoint, Redwood Hosted, and Redwood Dedicated at realistic concurrency. Measure p50/p90/p99, tail CPU/GPU usage, and cost per 1M tokens.
- Observability: verify per-route latency/cost breakdown, token-level traces, and ability to set alerting on quality regressions.
- Rollouts: validate canary traffic split, automatic rollback on eval regressions, and manual override ergonomics.
- Security: confirm KMS/HSM integration, VPC peering or private connectivity, and audit log granularity.

Battle-card snippets for AMs (30–60s soundbites):
- "Predictable end-to-end inference economics — because you can measure and change the unit drivers (batching, cache, model quant)."
- "Exportable rollout policies and evals so you can safely push model changes without a firefight when a product ship drops."
- "Private control plane options for regulated workloads — hardware boundaries without losing managed platform benefits."

Next steps & recommended assets to attach to buyer conversations:
- POC plan template (benchmarks + measurement checklist) — link to Confluence (see linked_artifacts).
- Short incident playbook showing how Redwood fallback policies preserved availability in a real customer incident (anonymized runbook).
- Cost-savings primer from Optimize showing typical % improvements from batching + quantization for mid-size NLP workloads.

Open questions / risks to monitor during GTM:
- Hyperscaler feature parity (they may add more inference knobs) — maintain a rolling feature gap doc.
- Pricing promotions from hyperscalers — update procurement playbook with counter offers and Dedicated commit options.
- Customer preference for single-vendor consolidation — emphasize multi-cloud routing and the small surface area for platform integration to reduce perceived vendor count.

Appendix: suggested POC metric targets (example):
- p99 under steady-state load: < 250ms for short-chat models; < 500ms for 8k-generation models on Dedicated in-region setups.
- Cost target: demonstrate >= 20% predictable unit-cost improvement vs hyperscaler-managed average over a 30-day realistic traffic sample (where batching and kv cache apply).
- Rollout safety: automatic rollback triggers on >2% regression in key prompt eval set quality or >25% increase in median latency during canary.

Notes to self / next revisions:
- Add anonymized customer case study for platform teams in fintech and healthcare.
- Expand the hyperscaler appendix with concrete billing line-item comparisons (if procurement will share billing exports).
- Solicit SRE feedback from teams who have run Redwood Dedicated migrations and incorporate operational runbook snippets.

End of doc.
